dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The work addresses Markowitz-style portfolio optimization, seeking the portfolio with the best return for a given risk and measuring portfolio quality via the Sharpe ratio, while modeling risk through the covariance matrix of historical asset returns and mapping a binary asset-selection formulation into a QUBO/Ising form suitable for quantum computation. A practical case study uses real market data from Yahoo Finance (via yfinance) over 2016–2023 to instantiate several small binary portfolio problems. The authors frame this as a finance optimization problem called portfolio optimization to which QAOA is applied.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The paper employs the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), presented as a prominent variational algorithm and practical NISQ application, implemented in a hybrid VQA framework where a parameterized quantum circuit is optimized by a classical routine. The QAOA circuit alternates problem and mixer unitaries with parameters (γ, β) optimized classically (using COBYLA) and is run both in an ideal, noiseless setting (statevector simulator) and with realistic noise models (IBM Manila and Lima via Qiskit), with noise described using quantum channels and Kraus operators. The portfolio problem is encoded via a QUBO-to-Ising mapping, starting from a binary formulation, and implemented using Qiskit and Qiskit Finance.

dimension_3_key_results.text: In noiseless simulations, QAOA is reported as converging to the correct portfolio for the 2-asset large-gap case, the 3-asset, and 4-asset problems, while failing in a 2-asset small-gap instance and only partially succeeding in the 5-asset case, where it did not quite converge but still yielded informative output. The authors observe that smaller energy gaps—associated with closer expected returns—correlate with convergence difficulties, and they regard performance for 2–4 qubits as satisfactory within the energy-gap restrictions. Under noisy simulations using IBM device models, QAOA performance degrades as expected: penalized states appear more often, the noisy small-gap 2-asset case can even underperform random guessing, but in other cases (e.g., some 2-qubit and 3-qubit instances) results remain worse than ideal yet still above random, with the Lima noise model performing better than Manila, possibly linked to T2 differences.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: Classically, the authors construct an efficient frontier from random portfolios to benchmark portfolio quality and compare QAOA’s performance against a random-guess baseline on the discrete search space. They report that in most small instances, both noiseless and some noisy QAOA runs achieve higher probability of the optimal state than random guessing, while in the noisy small-gap 2-asset case the QAOA-based strategy performs worse than random, with the green QAOA line falling below the cyan random baseline in their plots.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The paper emphasizes several limitations: at the algorithmic level, QAOA’s main restraint is the exponential cost and NP-hardness of optimizing its 2p parameters, and VQAs more broadly suffer from barren plateaus, including those induced by noise, which can make gradients vanish with system size. On the problem side, performance is sensitive to the energy spectrum; small energy gaps—linked to similar asset returns—make convergence harder, and the five-qubit portfolio instance is an unexplained outlier possibly related to the larger state space. Noise further limits performance by populating penalized states, rendering the expectation value of energy a poor performance metric in the noisy setting. Regarding hardware, real IBM devices are deemed non-viable for the study because queueing and calibration constraints would require an impractically large number of queued jobs (e.g., 16,380 queues for a four-qubit case), so the work is restricted to simulators and calibrated noise models. The authors also note that the better performance of the Lima noise model relative to Manila is only tentatively attributed to T2 differences, and they explicitly state that the five-qubit anomaly remains unclear.

dimension_6_future_work.text: Future research directions include testing QAOA modifications such as warm-starting and mixed-Hamiltonian techniques to improve convergence and solution quality, running larger simulations (e.g., six-qubit instances) to shed light on the five-qubit anomaly, and introducing a new evaluation metric based on the probability gap between the optimal and second-most-probable states. The authors also propose richer portfolio encodings by adding more qubits to represent weight probabilities instead of binary inclusion variables, and suggest exploring error-mitigation methods, such as those under development by IBM, to ameliorate noise effects in NISQ devices.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The thesis positions its main contribution as applying the QAOA variational algorithm—highlighted as a practical NISQ-era method—to a concrete finance optimization problem, namely portfolio optimization, using real market data, and systematically comparing ideal and noisy simulations under realistic IBM noise models. Within this framing that quantum computing has progressed beyond its earliest stages into an intermediate noisy era without full error correction, the work aims to empirically study whether QAOA can provide satisfactory approximate solutions on small portfolio instances and to characterize how noise and problem structure (e.g., energy gaps) affect performance.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the work is structured across chapters that cover quantum theory (circuit and adiabatic models), finance foundations, implementation, and conclusions, and provides standard definitions of qubits, gates, universal gate sets, adiabatic computation, noise channels, and readout errors to ground the implementation. The VQA framework and parameter-shift gradients are discussed, though the actual optimizer used is gradient-free (COBYLA), and the simulations explicitly distinguish statevector-based ideal runs from noisy QASM-based runs calibrated to IBM Manila and Lima noise models. Risk is measured via covariance matrices from historical prices, portfolio quality by the Sharpe ratio, and binary encoding is justified as making the problem more digestible as a QUBO. The implementation relies on Qiskit and Qiskit Finance, with explicit acknowledgment that real-device execution was impractical due to queueing and calibration constraints, which the authors treat as a methodological limitation of their experimental setup.
